caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores (normative deviation scores); infranormal defined as z < -1.96 (5th percentile); supranormal defined as z > 1.96 (95th percentile); intermediate values (within normal range) as -1.96 ≤ z ≤ 1.96; Average Deviation Scores (ADS) computed for CT, SA, SV, and globally across all measures
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper clearly defines the deviation metrics. Z-scores were computed by subtracting the estimated value from the raw value and dividing by the root mean square error of the model. Regional z-scores below -1.96 or above 1.96 were designated as infranormal or supranormal, corresponding to 5th and 95th percentiles. ADS were calculated by averaging regional z-scores.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: For each measure in each participant, we estimated the degree of normative deviation from the reference population mean as a z score computed by subtracting the estimated value from the raw value of that measure, and then dividing the difference by the root mean square error of the model. A positive or negative z score indicated that the value of the corresponding morphometric measure was higher or lower, respectively, than the normative mean. Per previous literature, we defined regional z scores as infranormal when below -1.96 or supranormal when above 1.96, corresponding to the 5th percentile and 95th percentile, respectively. Intermediate values (ie, z scores between -1.96 and 1.96) were designated as within normal range... We averaged the regional z scores in each participant to generate an average deviation score (ADS) for CT, SA, and SV.
caa6_deviation_metric.location: Haas2024.pdf.md: Methods / Computing Deviation Scores and Computation of Average Deviation Scores, L112-119

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Within the CHR-P group, linear regression models were used to assess associations between positive symptoms and IQ with each regional z score and each ADS, with age included as a variable in all regression models. Analyses were conducted with and without site as a random effect. Two-proportion z tests were used to examine group differences in the proportion of individuals with supra- or infranormal z scores. Linear support vector classification with 10-fold cross-validation was used to estimate diagnostic status (CHR-P vs healthy individuals and CHR-PC vs healthy individuals) using all regional z scores as input. Brain basis set (BBS) multivariable estimation modeling method was used to identify multivariate patterns of associations of regional z scores with IQ and positive symptoms. Analyses were repeated separately for CHR-PC and CHR-PNC subgroups. Sensitivity analyses included leave-one-site-out approach, alternate ADS definitions, medication status adjustment, and robustness testing with alternate normative models (GPR, GAMLSS) and parcellations (Schaeffer 400). All tests used Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons with significance at P < 0.05.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Individual-level variation in macroscale neuromorphometric measures in CHR-P was largely nested within healthy variation; extreme deviations were present in only a minority of CHR-P individuals at proportions similar to healthy individuals; regional z-scores had negligible value for predicting diagnosis, cognition, positive symptoms, or conversion status.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The distributions of z-scores and observed values of all regional neuromorphometric measures in CHR-P and healthy individuals had complete overlap. For any given region, the proportion of CHR-P individuals with infranormal or supranormal values was low (up to 11.42%) and similar to healthy individuals (<9.30%). Among all CHR-P, 74.63% had infranormal z-scores in at least one CT region, 62.76% in at least one SA region, and 40.00% in at least one SV region; corresponding proportions in healthy individuals were 71.71%, 62.25%, and 34.11%. Linear support vector classifiers using regional z-scores or observed data were unable to distinguish healthy individuals from CHR-P (z-scores AUC 0.53, observed AUC 0.56) or from CHR-PC (z-scores AUC 0.52, observed AUC 0.47). A significantly higher percentage of CHR-P had infranormal global ADS (χ²=12.82, P=6.85×10⁻⁴), SV ADS (χ²=5.68, P=0.02), and SA ADS (χ²=16.01, P=2.53×10⁻⁴) compared to healthy individuals. Within CHR-P, only SA ADS was associated with positive symptoms (β=-0.08, P=0.02) and IQ (β=0.09, P=0.02); global ADS was associated with IQ (β=0.10, P=0.01). These associations did not persist when site was included as a random effect for positive symptoms but remained for IQ. Converters (CHR-PC) had a higher percentage of infranormal values in temporal regions: 5.10% vs 0.89% healthy individuals for right inferior temporal thickness (χ²=15.34, P=0.01), and 7.01% vs 1.38% CHR-PNC for right banks superior temporal sulcus surface area (χ²=17.34, P=4.69×10⁻³). In CHR-PC, IQ was positively associated with SA ADS (β=0.26, P=0.02) and global ADS (β=0.21, P=0.05), persisting with site as random effect.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Multi-site data collection with different scanners and protocols, though site effects were accounted for via harmonization and leave-one-site-out analyses; cross-sectional neuroimaging data that do not capture potential longitudinal changes; residual site effects cannot be fully excluded
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: As is common with largescale studies, the data were collected at multiple sites using different scanners and protocols. Although we accounted for site effects using MRI data harmonization and tested the robustness of the results using leave-one-site-out analyses, residual effects cannot be fully excluded but are unlikely to have influenced the overall pattern of the results. The neuroimaging data of the individuals with CHR are cross-sectional and do not capture potentially longitudinal changes that may be more informative.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study tested robustness through multiple approaches: (1) alternate normative modeling algorithms (GPR, GAMLSS) and parcellations (Schaeffer 400 parcels, voxel-based); (2) subgroup analyses by CHR-P subsyndrome (APS, BIPS, GRD); (3) multiple alternate definitions of ADS (positive only, negative only, absolute values); (4) sensitivity to medication status (243 [18.63%] on antipsychotics); (5) leave-one-site-out cross-validation; (6) comparison of normative z-scores versus raw observed values for prediction. The Brain Basis Set (BBS) multivariate method was used to decompose neuroimaging measures into specific components before modeling. Traditional case-control comparisons replicated prior ENIGMA findings of small effect size CT reductions (<0.22) in CHR-P.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is the largest neuroimaging study of CHR-P using normative modeling, applying pre-trained models from the ENIGMA Lifespan Group's CentileBrain framework (N=37,407 reference) to the ENIGMA CHR-P Working Group sample (N=1340 CHR-P, N=1237 healthy). The study addressed three subgroups within CHR-P: attenuated psychotic symptoms (APS), brief intermittent psychotic symptoms (BIPS), and genetic risk and functional deterioration (GRD) syndromes. Positive symptoms were rated with SIPS (n=806) or CAARMS (n=534) and converted to z-scores for harmonization. IQ estimates were also z-score normalized across sites due to different instruments used. Follow-up data (mean 19.71±13.97 months) was available for 1097/1340 CHR-P individuals, with 157 (14.31%) converting to psychosis. The study found that macroscale brain morphometry may have limited utility as diagnostic biomarkers for psychosis risk, as individual variation was largely nested within the normative range. Code and normative models are publicly available at https://centilebrain.org (reference: Ge et al., BioRxiv 2023, doi:10.1101/2023.01.30.523509).
